title: [SPOILERS] [Reviews] My .02 on all the Best Picture Noms

commenti.body:
Any Anatomy of a Fall fan should consider checking out Otto Preminger's Anatomy of a Murder. The similarity in title is no coincidence! 

Respectfully, what did you feel was the theme of Oppenheimer? Do you feel like you understand him better after? Do you think we are meant to leave with an opinion on the man, or his role in the war? How did you come away feeling  about the nuclear bomb and his role in it's development?

 I understand this is a well loved movie, and I am not trying to rain on any parades, but I did not like this movie, and I am flummoxed by its praise.  I am hoping understanding what others liked about it will help me see what I missed.

Out of all the Best Picture nominees I’ve seen, I think Poor Things is the strongest, but this year I’ve sort of realized how much I enjoy Yorgos Lanthimos’s films. 

Oppenheimer I just don’t get the praise for. Maybe it’s because I read American Prometheus in 2022, but I absolutely hated the first half of the movie. It felt like a biopic parody the way it simplifies and quickly jumps from all these important moments in his pre-Los Alamos life. I understand why Nolan had to do that, there’s a lot you need to cram in that even 3 hours isn’t enough, but the execution just felt so poor to me. I couldn’t help but laugh in the theatre when he’s having sex with Jean for the first time and she has him read the Bhagavad Gita to her and he reads “the line” of all things. It just felt so ham fisted and on the nose. Speaking of which, I found that Jean and Kitty weren’t done justice in the movie and came off to me as rather one dimensional, almost caricature-like, though I think Emily Blunt and Florence Pugh were good with what they had to work with.

That said, I did the enjoy the movie more in the second half after the Trinity Test (and the constant build of music was finally over), but largely I found Oppenheimer to be dull after being so fascinated reading American Prometheus.

I went in fairly blind, so I think that could definitely have to do with it. I knew very little about the man, felt like i learned a lot, and i was enchanted by the story, but i buy here the book could make you frustrated with the film.

I think that there were a number of key themes/messages of the movie.

I think one is the weight of genius. And the weight of not being a genius. There's levels. Oppenheimer compared to the other scientists, the scientists compared to the chairman(blanking on his name), oppy compared to his friends who took his kid. etc.

Along with that, the weight of being greatness adjacent - his wives, friends, coworkers, etc.

Also, the sense of duty to what you were taught to believe, and your duty to what you do believe is another one.

Finally, the unintended consequences, and at what point are you faulted for it. "Near zero."..."zero...would be nice" also can speak to what happens after they drop the real bomb.
thanks for the suggestion I'll have to check it out!

I see, thank you!

Yeah I have very strong feelings about the bomb and just feel the movie really underplays the whole thing. But your explanation was great!
Anatomy of a Murder and Fall are kind of in conversation with one another. As a longtime fan of …Murder I thought it was very clever how Fall paid homage while also being about a lot of other stuff

THat's interesting, i see how you could leave that movie with that opinion. It certainly lets the audience know how the dropping was celebrated by the country at the time, but I would argue Nolan, particularly int he final scene paints a much more cynical view on the manhattan project - but I understand if you have strong personal feelings that build the lens of watching anything. That's what makes discussion worthwhile!

Yes, I understand this final scene was quite powerful for many. To me, I'm not a religious man, but to me the bomb is Evil. I cannot understand portraying its invention with anything less than harsh judgement. 

It is also deeply disturbing to me that we don't see what happened to Hiroshima and Nagasaki - most Americans have never seen the military's declassified footage of what happened after the bombs were dropped. 

Finally, and it's arguable whether to fault Nolan for this, but this film's success insures **this** portrayal of Oppenheimer and that period will live on in American's memories as 'what happened when America invented the bomb'. 

Yet the film has no math, no science, no discussion of the ethical constraints that ought to have been in place (and were in Europe, which is why they didn't pursue atomics). Nolan excludes these things from his narrative, which will leave an incorrect impression with 90% of its viewers. 

THAT SAID, Nolan is a master filmmaker and obviously this film is a huge accomplishment. I appreciate your sharing your point-of-view with me!!
